scope_note: Authoritative family-recognition backfill for the Hays/Central Texas learner. Restores missing Commelina and Tinantia family mappings, retains Tradescantia, and builds a three-genus visual framework emphasizing closed leaf sheaths, jointed/succulent nodes, 3-part flowers, filament hairs/staminodes, and capsules.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: In vegetation, start at the node: soft/fleshy jointed stems and alternate parallel-veined leaves whose bases form a conspicuous sheath around the stem. In flower, confirm 3 sepals + 3 petals, usually 6 stamens or a mixture of fertile stamens and staminodes, a superior 3-carpellate ovary, and a capsule.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Closed or strongly sheathing leaf base + succulent/jointed node + 3 sepals distinct from 3 petals + conspicuous filament hairs or differentiated stamens/staminodes + superior ovary + capsule.
core_characters: Annual or perennial herbs, often somewhat succulent, with conspicuous nodes and internodes.
Adventitious roots may develop at lower nodes.
Leaves alternate, simple, parallel-veined, with a basal sheath that is commonly closed or nearly closed around the stem.
Inflorescences are cymose; Commelina encloses them in a conspicuous folded spathe.
Flowers have 3 sepals and 3 free petals; symmetry ranges from radial in local Tradescantia to strongly bilateral in Commelina and Tinantia.
Stamens are often 6, but some may be sterile staminodes; filament hairs can be extremely conspicuous.
Fruit a loculicidal capsule; seed number and capsule-valve pattern vary by genus.
Petals are ephemeral and may wilt/liquefy within hours, so vegetative and fruit characters matter.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach all Commelinaceae as 3 equal blue petals; Commelina and Tinantia are strongly zygomorphic with unequal petals.
Do not teach 6 fertile stamens as absolute; Commelina erecta has 3 fertile stamens + 3 staminodes.
Do not teach filament hairs as universal; Commelina has glabrous filaments while local Tradescantia/Tinantia can have showy beadlike hairs.
Do not identify the family from grass-like leaves alone; inspect the sheath, node, and flower.
Do not create separate learner cards for the old Commelina erecta variety rows without a dedicated taxonomic reason.

fastest_cues: Flower usually radial in the local spiderwort anchors.
Three broad, roughly equal blue/violet/pink petals.
Six fertile stamens in the strongest local anchor, T. gigantea.
No enclosing folded heart-shaped spathe like Commelina.
Tradescantia.teaching_anchor: Tradescantia gigantea gives the cleanest family anatomy: closed sheath, 3 sepals, 3 equal petals, 6 fertile hairy stamens, superior 3-locular ovary, 3-valved capsule.

fastest_cues: Inflorescence enclosed in a conspicuous folded spathe/pocket.
Two large blue upper/posterior petals + one much smaller pale/white lower petal.
Three fertile stamens + three showy staminodes/antherodes.
Fruit develops largely hidden back inside the spathe.
Commelina.teaching_anchor: Commelina erecta is the best staminode lesson and the best genus to teach the term spathe.

fastest_cues: Strongly bilateral flower but without Commelina's folded pocket-like spathe.
Two large blue lateral petals + one much smaller white lower petal.
All six stamens fertile but strongly heteromorphic.
Multiple stamens bear dense beadlike filament hairs, giving the flower a fuzzy face.
Persistent sepals conceal the developing 3-valved capsule.
Tinantia.teaching_anchor: Tinantia anomala is the perfect bridge between Tradescantia and Commelina: zygomorphic like Commelina, but six fertile hairy stamens rather than three fertile + three sterile.

fast_key: Soft jointed herb + sheathing parallel-veined leaves + 3 sepals/3 petals -> strongly consider Commelinaceae.
Radial flower + 3 similar broad petals + 6 fertile hairy stamens -> Tradescantia framework.
Folded green pocket/spathe + 2 huge blue petals + tiny white lower petal + 3 fertile stamens/3 staminodes -> Commelina erecta.
No folded Commelina pocket + bilateral blue flower + fuzzy heteromorphic set of 6 fertile stamens -> Tinantia anomala.
Grass-like vegetative plant with a ligule and typical grass spikelets -> Poaceae instead.
Iris-like 6 similar tepals + inferior ovary -> reconsider Iridaceae.

Poaceae.confusion: Vegetative spiderwort/dayflower can look grass-like because of parallel venation and sheathing leaf bases.
Poaceae.tie_breaker: Commelinaceae stems are often fleshy/jointed and lack a grass ligule; flowers are showy 3-sepal + 3-petal structures rather than spikelets with glumes/lemmas/paleas.

Iridaceae.tie_breaker: Iridaceae commonly has 6 tepals that are more alike and an inferior ovary; Commelinaceae has clearly different sepals vs petals, a superior ovary and conspicuous sheathing nodes.
